newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ex-Polish Communist ruler unveils book in West.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Polish Communist ruler unveils book in West.

text.p: Wojciech Jaruzelski, facing trial for the 1970 killings of protesting workers, defended his record as Poland's last Cold War-era Communist ruler on Wednesday by presenting his memoirs to the capitalist West.

Jaruzelski, 73, the architect of martial law which tried to smash Eastern Europe's first independent trade union Solidarity, presented a German translation of his best-selling 1992 book arguing he had averted the greater disaster of Soviet invasion.
Once the most powerful man in Poland, a quiet-spoken Jaruzelski, told Western journalists at Frankfurt Book Fair not to judge him and other former Eastern Bloc leaders too harshly.

"Every political leader had a narrow range of play, whether you were (ex-Soviet president) Gorbachev, (ex-Czech leader Gustav) Husak or (East German leader Erich) Honecker," said Jaruzelski, still wearing his trademark dark glasses.
"But I am more convinced than ever before martial law was the lesser of two evils" he said.
Jaruzelski said he hoped the book, which sold 300,000 copies in Poland, would help westerners understand the limited options open to him and that he did the best he could under the circumstances.

"Many politicians today suffer from loss of memory. But I am not saying I was a different person then," said Jaruzelski. "I believed in protecting the Socialist state from destruction and that Socialism could be reformed".

Since Jaruzelski abdicated after Poland's first post-war free elections in 1990, he has been the subject of several investigations into the 1970 killings, his imposition of martial law and missing Communist party files.

But the liklihood of a conviction looks slim. Poland's parliament, dominated by former communists, has recommended he should not be tried for the 1981 martial law declaration, which led to thousand of arrests and some deaths.
Earlier this year he went on trial with 11 others, mainly former security and army officers accused of instigating the shootings of 44 protesting workers in 1970.
The trial could be the biggest in the nation's history with with 1,000 witnesses likely to be summoned. But the proceedings have been postponed for further investigations.
Jaruzelski's book entitled "Martial Law -- Why?" opens with his sleepless nights and thoughts of suicide under immense pressure from Moscow to crack down on Solidarity.

In Poland it became a best-seller and opinion polls show most Poles accept his argument martial law was the lesser evil. Former Soviet officials have since confirmed invasion plans had in fact been drawn up.
The 479-page German translation of his book is entitled: "Behind the corridors of power" and was published by Militzke in Leipzig, east Germany's first independent publishers.
The first edition in Germany had a printing run of 6,000 -- modest compared to the 300,000 sold back at home. The German version is the first foreign translation of his book to be published.
